1.title: Evaluation Metrics, Datasets and Frameworks
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Evaluation Metrics, Datasets and Frameworks. This module covers evaluation metrics, datasets and frameworks. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. How to turn requirements into measurable success criteria and metrics. How to build evaluation datasets. Mixed methodologies: code-graded, L L M (large language model)-graded, human-graded. An evaluation framework that runs on every change.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Defines "Good" for a Bank's Claims-Triage Assistant
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Defines "Good" for a Bank's Claims-Triage Assistant. The bank says "it must be accurate, fast, cheap and safe". Lumen turns each word into a number and a test.

1.title: Success Criteria and Metrics
1.text: Success Criteria and Metrics. Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant. Most systems need several dimensions at once.

1.title: Success Criteria and Metrics, continued
1.text: Success Criteria and Metrics, continued. Accuracy or task fidelity. Example metric and target: ninety-five percent correct triage category on a held-out set. How to measure: Exact match against labels. Faithfulness (R A G). Example metric and target: ninety-eight percent of claims supported by cited passages. How to measure: L L M-judge or citation check. Retrieval quality. Example metric and target: recall@twenty at least ninety-seven percent. How to measure: Labeled relevant passages. Consistency. Example metric and target: Same answer for paraphrases. How to measure: Similarity across paraphrase sets. Latency. Example metric and target: p ninety-five under three seconds; time to first token under one second. How to measure: Timing logs. Cost. Example metric and target: Under zero dollars and two cents per case. How to measure: Token and price accounting. Safety. Example metric and target: Under zero point one percent of outputs flagged harmful. How to measure: Classifier or judge on samples.

1.title: Success Criteria and Metrics, continued
1.text: Success Criteria and Metrics, continued. Security. Example metric and target: zero successful injection attacks in the red-team set. How to measure: Adversarial tests. Reliability. Example metric and target: Error and timeout rate below zero point five percent. How to measure: Production metrics.

1.title: Success Criteria and Metrics, continued
1.text: Success Criteria and Metrics, continued. The figure shows this: Evaluation dimensions: accuracy, faithfulness, retrieval, consistency, latency, cost, safety and security, each with a metric and a grading method. Metric families: task-specific (F one, B L E U, R O U G E), generic (accuracy, precision, recall), operational (latency, uptime), safety (flag rate), qualitative scales (Likert or rubric) alongside numbers. Define the threshold before you test, and which metrics are gates (must pass) versus tracked.

1.title: Success Criteria and Metrics, continued
1.text: Success Criteria and Metrics, continued. Precision and recall trade off: choose by the cost of a miss versus a false alarm (for example fraud flags). Exam tip: "Accurate" is not a metric. The architect's answer states specific numeric criteria on a held-out dataset, across several dimensions.

1.title: Evaluation Datasets
1.text: Evaluation Datasets. The figure shows this: An evaluation dataset combines expert-written cases, production samples, edge and adversarial cases and synthetic cases, split into development and held-out sets.

1.title: Evaluation Datasets, continued
1.text: Evaluation Datasets, continued. Expert-written golden cases. Core behavior with trusted labels. Production samples (consented, redacted). Real distribution; update regularly. Edge cases. Empty, very long or irrelevant input, sarcasm, mixed signals, ambiguous items where humans disagree. Adversarial and red-team cases. Prompt injection, jailbreaks, data-exfiltration attempts. Synthetic cases. Scale and coverage; generated by a model and reviewed. Mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases. Volume over polish: many automatically graded items beat a few hand-graded ones, but label quality matters; review disagreements. Keep a held-out set untouched by prompt tuning to avoid overfitting to the dev set.

1.title: Evaluation Datasets, continued
1.text: Evaluation Datasets, continued. Version datasets; add every production failure as a new case (a regression set). Avoid leakage: do not put eval answers in the prompt or few-shot examples. Start small (about twenty representative cases) to find big problems fast, then grow.

1.title: Mixed Methodologies
1.text: Mixed Methodologies. Code-graded (exact match, regex, schema, unit checks). Strength: Fast, cheap, reliable. Weakness: Only for checkable answers. Use for: Classification, extraction, format, tool-call correctness. L L M-graded (rubric, Likert, binary). Strength: Scales; handles nuance. Weakness: Needs calibration; can be biased. Use for: Tone, faithfulness, completeness, helpfulness. Human-graded. Strength: Highest validity. Weakness: Slow and costly. Use for: Calibration, high-stakes review, edge cases. Semantic similarity (embeddings, R O U G E). Strength: Compares to a reference. Weakness: Weak on correctness. Use for: Summaries, paraphrase consistency. Operational telemetry. Strength: Real behavior. Weakness: Not about correctness. Use for: Latency, cost, errors. L L M-judge practice. Use a detailed rubric with clear criteria; ask for reasoning first, then a score or pass or fail.

1.title: Mixed Methodologies, continued
1.text: Mixed Methodologies, continued. Prefer binary or small scales; use a different model from the generator as judge when possible. Calibrate against a human-labeled sample and recheck periodically. Judge outcomes, not one fixed path (agent paths vary).

1.title: An Evaluation Framework
1.text: An Evaluation Framework. The figure shows this: An evaluation framework: dataset and metrics, run, grade with mixed methods, compare against the baseline, gate the release, and add new failures back. Dataset and metrics with thresholds. Harness that runs the system (prompt version, model, parameters, retrieval config) on every case and records outputs, latency and tokens. Graders by method; store scores per case. Compare to a baseline (current production) on the same cases. Gate the release (C I): block if a gated metric regresses.

1.title: An Evaluation Framework, continued
1.text: An Evaluation Framework, continued. Online evals after release: sampled production scoring, thumbs, correction rates. Feed back new failures into the dataset. Evaluate components separately (retrieval, generation, tools) and end to end. For agents, evaluate outcomes and also tool-use efficiency and safety; add human testing for what automation misses. Security evals are part of the suite (injection, tool abuse); safety evals test refusals and harmful-output rates. Exam tip: "Accurate" is not a metric: state numeric targets on a held-out dataset across several dimensions. Exam tip: Keep a held-out set untouched by tuning, and add every production failure to the regression set.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Criteria: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant; multidimensional. Dimensions: Accuracy, faithfulness, retrieval, consistency, latency, cost, safety, security. Dataset: Golden, production, edge, adversarial, synthetic; dev and held-out; versioned; regression set. Methods: Code (checkable), L L M judge (nuance, calibrated), human (calibration, high stakes). Judge: Rubric, reasoning first, different model, calibrate. Framework: Dataset to run to grade to compare to baseline to gate to online to feed back. Start: About twenty cases, then grow.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A client requires the assistant to be "accurate and fast." Which restatement is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Specific, measurable criteria on a defined dataset are testable.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which grading method is most appropriate for checking that extracted invoice totals match labeled values? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Checkable answers should use fast, reliable code grading.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An L L M judge is used to score the empathy of replies. What practice improves reliability? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Rubrics, reasoning, a separate judge and calibration make L L M grading dependable.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Prompt changes keep improving the dev-set score but production quality does not improve. What is the likely cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Tuning against the same cases inflates scores; use a held-out set.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two belong in an evaluation dataset? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and C. Realistic production-like cases and difficult edge or adversarial cases reveal the weaknesses that a clean sample would hide.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A production failure is found. What should the team do with it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Every production failure becomes a permanent regression case, so later changes are tested against it before release.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A R A G assistant's answers sometimes include claims not in the retrieved passages. Which metric tracks this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Faithfulness measures the share of claims supported by the retrieved passages, which is exactly the grounding problem described.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. How should fraud flags be tuned when missing fraud is far costlier than a false alarm? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Choose the metric trade-off by the cost of each error type.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Which is the best first sample size for fast feedback on a new agent system? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A small first sample of about twenty cases reveals large effects early, and the set can grow as patterns emerge.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Agent runs take different valid paths to the same result. How should they be graded? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Agents can take different valid paths, so grading should check the outcome and key constraints rather than one fixed sequence.

1.title: Practice Question 11
1.text: Question eleven. A team wants an eval that catches regressions before every release. What is the right mechanism? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Running the dataset in continuous integration and gating on metrics against the baseline protects every release from regressions.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eleven answers. Question one: D. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: D. Question five: B and C. Question six: A. Question seven: C. Question eight: C. Question nine: D. Question ten: C. Question eleven: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
